opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing people outside the art world often don't appreciate is what a style actually is for an artist. It's not a filter or a preset. For most of the artists we've talked to, and we've talked to well over a thousand of them at this point, their style is the product of ten, fifteen, twenty years of work. It's every choice they've made about line weight, color, composition, what to leave out. It's shaped by their training, their influences, their life experiences. In a very real sense, the style *is* the artist. When someone looks at a piece and says, "Oh, that's so-and-so's work," that recognition is the culmination of a career.

So when a model can be fine-tuned on a few dozen of their images in an afternoon, and then anyone can type in their name and generate hundreds of images that look like theirs, several things happen at once. Economically, the obvious one: clients who would have commissioned them now just generate something "in the style of" for free. We've seen artists lose a large share of their income almost overnight. But the identity piece is, I think, even more painful. Their name becomes a prompt keyword. Search their name online and you find a flood of AI-generated images that aren't theirs, some of them quite bad, some of them things they would never make, and those images get attributed to them. Their own work gets buried under the imitations.

And there's a deeper loss too. Many artists told us that it made them question whether they want to keep making art at all, or at least keep sharing it publicly, because every piece they post is effectively more training data for the thing that's replacing them. Younger artists ask, why would I spend fifteen years developing a voice if it can be taken from me in a weekend? That's what really worries me. It's not only harm to individuals today; it's the pipeline of human creativity going forward. If people stop investing in developing distinctive styles, we all lose something.

That's a big part of why we built Glaze and later Nightshade. Artists were asking us for something, anything, that gave them back a little agency over how their work gets used. It's not a perfect solution, but when someone's identity is on the line, giving them some way to fight back matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes artists’ close identification with their styles, but never contrasts that with Ben Zhao’s more detached relationship to his research papers.

r002.rationale: It says anyone can use an artist’s name as a prompt to generate images in their style, and describes the resulting loss of control over how that identity is used.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says searches for an artist’s name can surface generated images that are not theirs and become attributed to them.

r004.rationale: It says AI-generated imitations flood searches for artists’ names and bury their own work.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it helps to start with what style actually is for an artist, because I don't think most people outside the art world appreciate it. For a working artist, style isn't a filter or a look you pick off a shelf. It's the accumulation of years, sometimes decades, of choices. How you handle light, how you handle color, the way you draw a hand or a face, what you leave out. It's the thing that makes someone look at a piece and say, oh, that's hers, that's his, without seeing a signature. It is, quite literally, the artist's identity in the marketplace and in the community. Commissions come because of it. Galleries and studios hire because of it. Students follow you because of it.

So when a model can be fine-tuned on maybe twenty or thirty of your pieces scraped off ArtStation or DeviantArt, and then anybody can type your name into a prompt and get something that is, to a casual eye, indistinguishable from your work, the thing that gets taken isn't one image. It's the whole thing. It's the reason people came to you in the first place.

And we heard this directly. When we started working with artists before Glaze, the stories were remarkably consistent. People would find their name being used as a prompt keyword, thousands of times, and then their own work would get buried in search results underneath the imitations. Clients would say, well, I can just generate it in your style now, why would I pay you. Some artists talked about feeling like they'd been erased, that someone had taken their voice and was speaking with it. A few of them just stopped posting entirely, which, for someone whose livelihood depends on being visible, is a kind of professional death.

The part I find especially cruel is the asymmetry. It took them fifteen years to build that. It takes an afternoon and a consumer GPU to copy it. And unlike a song or a specific painting, style has basically no legal protection. Copyright doesn't cover it. So there's no recourse, no takedown you can file. Which is really why we ended up where we did, trying to give artists a technical lever when the legal and policy levers just weren't there.

r001.rationale: The response describes artists’ styles as part of their identity, but does not contrast this with Ben Zhao’s more detached relationship to his research papers.

r002.rationale: It says others can prompt a model with an artist’s name to generate work that looks indistinguishable from theirs, using the recognizable identity the artist built.

r003.rationale: It describes artists’ names being used as prompt keywords to generate imitations, linking their names to images they did not create.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says artists’ own work can be buried in search results beneath imitations when people search for their names.

astra-6.text:
I think people often hear “style” and think of it as a visual effect—a palette, a particular way of drawing a line. But for an artist, it can be the product of decades of experimentation, of figuring out what they want to say and how they want to say it. It’s how people recognize their work. In that sense, it’s deeply connected to their identity.

So when a model can reproduce that recognizable style on demand, without their involvement or consent, the loss goes beyond a commission or a paycheck. Suddenly, something they spent their life developing becomes something anyone can summon by typing their name. And the artist has no control over what gets made or what messages that work conveys.

That doesn’t mean the model has reproduced the person or their lived experience. But it can reproduce enough of the outward expression that audiences may stop seeing the distinction. You’re still there, you’re still creating, but your own name and visual language can start to point to a flood of work you had nothing to do with. That’s a profound loss of agency over how you’re represented in the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses artists’ style and identity but does not contrast that with Ben Zhao’s relationship to his research papers.

r002.rationale: It says models can reproduce an artist’s recognizable style without consent, leaving the artist with no control over what is made or what messages it conveys.

r003.rationale: It states that an artist’s name and visual language can become associated with a flood of work they had nothing to do with.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention image searches for an artist’s name or AI imitations displacing the artist’s own work in those results.

sol-6.1.text:
For an artist, style is much more than a particular color palette or a set of brushstrokes. It’s the result of years of experimentation, of figuring out what they want to say and how they want to say it. It’s how people recognize their work, and often it’s deeply connected to how they understand themselves.

So when someone takes their work and trains a model to imitate that style, the impact goes beyond losing a commission. Suddenly, anybody can generate something that looks like their work, attach their name to it, and make it say things they would never choose to say. The artist has lost some control over this visual identity they’ve spent their life building.

And I think that’s something we miss when we frame this purely as a question of productivity or copyright. For the artist, it can feel like something intensely personal has been taken away, and they have very little ability to stop it.

r001.rationale: The response describes artists’ deep personal connection to their styles but does not compare it with Ben Zhao’s relationship to his research papers.

r002.rationale: It says anyone can generate work that looks like the artist’s and make it say things they would not choose, leaving the artist with less control over that visual identity.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says someone can attach the artist’s name to generated work they did not create.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention imitations replacing the artist’s own work in image searches for their name.
